transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-13
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Delgado (Velaris Eng Lead), Asha Nair (Velaris SRE), Tom Li (Velaris Product)

Auto-generated sections:
Topics: [intro, streaming behavior, params, retry/backoff, Optimize suggestions, next steps]
Action items (auto): Jordan to send pricing and sandbox, Priya to share Optimize export.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan, i'm the ae on this account and with me is priya our se who will take most of the tech walkthroughs. how's everyone doing?
[00:18] Mark: good thanks, excited. quick ask — we wanna see streaming and how retries look in practice. we've seen some jitter in our current setup.
[00:30] Priya: great, i'll jump into a live sandbox demo, show streaming chunks, then we'll toggle params like temperature, max_tokens, and show a failover scenario. i'll also show the Console Optimize tab where we have batching and caching recommendations.
[00:45] Asha: quick note, we're interested in token costs, so anything you can show about per-token breakdowns or console costs will be helpful.
[01:05] Priya: definitely. in the hosted api we show token-level cost rollups per call and you can see it in the Console -> Billing -> Token breakdown, and Optimize will suggest quantization and batching if it fits your workload.
[01:25] Tom: when you say batching, is that client-side or server-side? we have short messages but high qps.
[01:38] Priya: good question. Redwood uses continuous batching in the runtime — server-side batching groups compatible requests to improve throughput. you can also enable a client-side buffer for small bursts. Optimize suggests the right batch size by looking at latency SLOs and traffic histograms.
[01:58] Mark: hmm ok. show us a streaming example.
[02:05] Priya: sure. i'm starting a chat -> generate call in the sandbox now. watch the stream come back as tokens in partial events.
[02:22] [PRIYA shares screen, runs curl and nodejs example]
[02:35] Priya: you can see the SSE chunks — first chunk is usually the preamble and then katex, oh sorry not katex — the answer body. sometimes transcription shows k-v cash instead of kv cache, you'll see that in our docs occasionally.
[02:52] Mark: out loud: so if a chunk drops, do we re-request the whole response or do you have a resume mechanism?
[03:05] Priya: currently streaming is best-effort. if a connection resets we recommend idempotent requests with an interaction id so clients can resume or re-ask. for long-running chats we persist KV (key-value) cache server-side for hot window sessions so a reconnect can rehydrate. note: our public hosted offering preserves short-term kv cache for the session lifetime.
[03:30] Asha: is that configurable? we have GDPR constraints and want max retention of 24 hours.
[03:40] Priya: yes, retention is configurable in Private/Dedicated. Hosted has default short retention but we can discuss specific retention windows for enterprise contracts — follow-up with security docs.
[03:55] Tom: how are retries handled when a request gets a 502?
[04:02] Priya: recommended pattern: exponential backoff + jitter, capped retries (2-3). important to use idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations or apply server-side dedupe where possible. also fallbacks: route to a cheaper model variant or smaller sequence len model automatically — that's in routing policies.
[04:25] Jordan: i'll add we'll send our retry sample code in the quickstart repo.
[04:34] Mark: can you show a failure and the retry in action?
[04:40] Priya: yep. i'm going to throttle the connection in the sandbox to emulate an intermittent 502.
[04:52] [screen: Priya triggers a simulated error then replays request with retry logic]
[05:15] Priya: notice how the client applies a backoff and then we get a second success response — token stream resumes from scratch, unless you implement resume logic, which requires storing the last-offset on the client.
[05:36] Asha: does resume rely on server-side partials?
[05:40] Priya: we don't provide a byte-range resume for token streams today; best practice is idempotency and saving partial results client-side. we do persist KV and context keys for session-level rehydration.
[05:58] Tom: you mentioned model variants for fallback. what's the perf/cost trade there?
[06:05] Priya: smaller variants save cost but may change output quality. Optimize will run a few prompts across variants and recommend a default plus a cheaper fallback. you can set routing policies: low-latency pool vs cost-saver pool. if latency SLOs are breached, we fallback to the cost-saver or a cached response depending on policy.
[06:30] Mark: show us the Console Optimize suggestions.
[06:36] [screen: Console -> Optimize tab visible, suggestions list appears]
[06:45] Priya: Optimize flagged high token inflation in a few prompts. recommended actions: reduce max_tokens where appropriate, apply a stop sequence to trim generative drift, and add presence penalty to avoid repetitive tokens. it also suggested a batching window of 30ms for your qps profile.
[07:10] Mark: presence penalty? can you give an example?
[07:14] Priya: it's a tunable that increases the likelihood of introducing new tokens rather than repeating. a value between 0 and 1.2 is common. try small increments e.g., 0.2. but this can change semantics so test with your prompt set.
[07:34] Tom: about token accounting — does console show cost per endpoint per route?
[07:40] Priya: yes, console routes map to model usage and you can see token counts per route, per API key, and per model. you can also slice by prompt sets in reports if you tag requests with metadata.
[07:56] Asha: any tips to reduce costs quickly?
[08:00] Priya: quick wins: 1) use stop sequences, 2) set tighter max_tokens and clamp generation, 3) use a smaller model for pre/post-processing or candidate rerank stages, 4) leverage prefix caching for FAQ-like stable prompts.
[08:18] Mark: we have a multi-turn assistant, how do we manage cumulative token growth?
[08:25] Priya: use summarized memory or chunked context. Redwood supports prefix/KV cache so you can store embeddings or compressed summaries server-side and only send a short context. Console has an Optimize pattern for conversation rollups.
[08:45] Jordan: note for the AE side — we'll include our conversation rollup pattern in the doc bundle.
[08:52] Mark: what's the SLA for hosted?
[08:55] Jordan: hosted api has an availability target in our public docs; for enterprise we can put stronger SLA in Dedicated. we'll attach the SLA matrix in the follow-up packet.
[09:10] Tom: any red flags we should be aware of when migrating from our current vendor?
[09:15] Priya: typical gotchas: 1) mis-sized batch settings can increase latency, 2) forgetting idempotency keys leads to duplicate side-effects, 3) over-reliance on long context without summarization increases cost. we recommend a staged pilot with traffic replay.
[09:34] Mark: traffic replay — can you ingest our logs to replay?
[09:39] Priya: yes, we can run a replay in a sandbox to produce a perf baseline. we'll need sample traffic shape and top prompts.
[09:50] Asha: ok that aligns with our SRE playbook. about security — do you have SOC2 and audit logs?
[09:58] Jordan: yes SOC 2 type 2; hosted has audit logs and API key role scoping. for advanced key management and customer-owned keys, Private or Dedicated is recommended. we'll attach the security whitepaper.
[10:15] Tom: any particular notes about idempotency keys format?
[10:20] Priya: just use UUIDs or deterministic hashes of request body. include them in the x-redwood-idempotency header and log them. backend will dedupe within the configured window.
[10:35] Mark: can you demonstrate a few param swaps? like temperature/ top_p change on same prompt to see output variance and token delta?
[10:44] Priya: yep. i'm going to run the same prompt at temp 0.0, temp 0.7 and temp 1.2 and show differences and tokens consumed.
[11:00] [PRIYA runs three generations side-by-side, shows token counters in Console]
[11:25] Priya: temp 0.0 deterministic — fewer creative tokens; temp 0.7 more varied; temp 1.2 we get more verbose and slightly longer generations hence higher token usage. Console shows delta in average tokens per call.
[11:45] Mark: top_p vs temp — best practice?
[11:50] Priya: temp controls randomness across distribution; top_p (nucleus sampling) clamps to cumulative probability mass. together they can be tuned — start with temp 0.6 top_p 0.9 for balanced outputs.
[12:05] Asha: about streaming chunk sizes — do you control chunk size server-side?
[12:10] Priya: we expose a chunking param; by default chunks are around 16-64 tokens but it varies by model and tokenizer. smaller chunks mean more SSE events but slightly higher overhead; larger chunks reduce events but increase perceived latency for first token.
[12:30] Tom: i saw a log entry in our environment where model latency spiked with long prompts; is there pre-warming?
[12:36] Priya: runtime supports warm pools and reserved capacity on Dedicated. for hosted you can also keep a warm session alive with occasional heartbeats if your SLA allows. Optimize will point out cold start patterns.
[12:55] Mark: walk me through a typical canary for a new model version.
[13:02] Priya: we suggest canary with route-level rollout: 1% traffic to new model with validation hooks in Console, run evals on a prompt set, monitor quality metrics and token cost, then ramp to 10/25/100% with automatic rollback on regressions. Console supports canary lanes and A/B baselines.
[13:30] Jordan: anything from procurement side?
[13:32] Tom: timeline — we'd like a pilot in the next 2 weeks and possibly a POC to prove tokens/costs.
[13:40] Jordan: that works. we'll send pilot pricing and sandbox access.
[13:45] Mark: a couple deep questions from our infra team — how do you handle backpressure when qps surges?
[13:52] Priya: runtime has queue depth controls and you can set per-route concurrency limits. also token budgeting per api-key to prevent runaway cost. when a surge happens we can prioritize based on tier (SLA) and return 429s for lower tiers. you'll see these controls in Console -> Routes.
[14:15] Asha: will a 429 cause a retry loop?
[14:20] Priya: clients should treat 429s as rate limiting signals and backoff. our sample SDKs implement an exponential backoff with jitter and respect retry-after headers.
[14:36] Mark: what about partial responses stored server-side?
[14:40] Priya: we persist session state and key-value context but not partial token streams for resume. resume requires client checkpoints.
[14:54] Tom: do you support tool-calling/function-calls?
[14:58] Priya: yes, hosted chat supports structured function/tool calling and streaming of function arguments as blocks. be mindful of how you handle idempotency of tool results.
[15:15] Mark: can you show a console trace for a single failing request?
[15:19] [PRIYA navigates to Console -> Traces, shows a trace with latencies and logs]
[15:40] Priya: here we can see tokenization time, kernel execution, and net latency. this helps pinpoint bottlenecks. sometimes the model kernel can be the bottleneck for very long sequences.
[15:58] Asha: last security thing — do you provide logs for GDPR export?
[16:03] Jordan: yes, we provide request-level logs and you can request data exports. for hosted there is an export process; for Private we provide direct access to logs. we'll include the process in the security packet.
[16:22] Tom: customer's curious — does Optimize automatically change live routing or only suggest?
[16:28] Priya: Optimize suggests and you can opt-in for automatic application of conservative suggestions. changes that affect quality require an explicit opt-in, by default it's advisory only.
[16:45] Mark: how does prefix caching work for question-answering?
[16:50] Priya: prefix caching stores the encoded KV cache for a commonly asked prefix so subsequent similar requests reuse the prefix and only send delta tokens. big wins for FAQ-like traffic.
[17:10] Tom: any nuance with quantization that affects streaming?
[17:15] Priya: quantization reduces memory and can slightly change latencies. it can introduce small quality diffs; Optimize flags prompts where quantization regressions could matter and suggests float fallback for those routes.
[17:34] Mark: competitor question — we use another provider today, and they tout lower latency; how should we benchmark?
[17:40] Priya: replay your traffic in sandbox with identical prompts and measure p50/p95 latencies and tokens. we can run a side-by-side benchmark and share a cost/lantency matrix.
[18:00] Jordan: we'll include a benchmark spreadsheet template.
[18:07] Asha: any best practices for idempotency window length?
[18:12] Priya: depends on your operation. for UI interactions 30-60s is common; for background jobs you might want longer dedupe windows. the backend dedupe config is adjustable on Dedicated.
[18:30] Mark: show a sample of the retry code from your SDKs.
[18:34] Priya: pulling up the node sdk sample...
[18:40] [PRIYA shows code, including retry decorator and idempotency header usage]
[19:02] Priya: note we also support streaming in websockets and SSE. websocket clients can buffer incoming token events and handle reconnections with the same idempotency approach.
[19:22] Tom: any gotchas for mobile clients?
[19:26] Priya: mobile networks are flaky — recommend short timeouts, local buffering, and sending compact contexts. also prefer smaller chunk sizes to get early first-byte.
[19:42] Mark: let's talk about the pilot scope. we want to measure cost per 1M messages and p95 latency for our assistant. how should we set that up?
[19:50] Priya: we'll set up a sandbox with traffic replay. collect baseline from your current provider, run identical replay on Redwood hosted sandbox, and we'll produce a side-by-side report including tokens, costs, and tail latencies.
[20:10] Jordan: action items recap at the end.
[20:12] Tom: one more quick question — if we want to reduce output tokens without breaking UX, any UX tips?
[20:18] Priya: control verbosity with max_tokens, stop sequences, and in-turn summarization after each exchange. also use post-generation pruning when appropriate.
[20:35] Mark: okay that was helpful, thanks.
[20:40] Priya: quick demo of a failure-mode fallback — we're going to flip routing so this route goes to a cheaper model and show a graceful downgrade.
[20:50] [PRIYA changes route setting to cost-saver pool, triggers request]
[21:10] Priya: you can see slightly different phrasing but overall preserved intent; Console shows a flag that this was a fallback event and logs the policy.
[21:30] Asha: do you surface fallback counts in metrics?
[21:33] Priya: yes, Console metrics include fallback_count per route and reason codes. you can alert on fallback spikes.
[21:48] Tom: any recommended thresholds for alerting?
[21:52] Priya: depends on your tolerance; many customers alert if fallback_rate > 1% of traffic or if p95 latency > SLA threshold.
[22:08] Mark: let's recap next steps.
[22:12] Jordan: recapping: 1) Jordan sends pilot pricing + sandbox creds and quickstart docs by 2025-11-18; 2) Priya shares Optimize export, batching guide, and sample retry code (by 2025-11-17); 3) Velaris provides traffic shape and top 50 prompts (by 2025-11-19); 4) schedule kickoff week of 2025-11-24 for baseline replay. sound right?
[22:38] Mark: yes.
[22:41] Tom: any outstanding procurement concerns?
[22:44] Jordan: procurement usually wants security docs and SLA — we'll attach the security whitepaper and the SLA matrix.
[23:00] Asha: thanks, that helps — we'll review and follow up.
[23:06] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll email the packet and link to the sandbox.
[23:12] Priya: quick note — i'll include a small script you can run to replay traffic into the sandbox.
[23:20] Mark: appreciated.
[23:23] Jordan: all right, end of demo, thanks folks.

(Transcript ends)
